Scoring conventions reorder adaptation policies in streaming anomaly detection

Dhruvil Amit Shah
Independent Researcher · contactshahdhruvil@gmail.com · ORCID 0009-0008-2988-5216
Preprint · September 2026, revised November 2026
Code and data: https://github.com/DhruvilShah22/drift-aware-anomaly-detection · License: CC BY 4.0
Cite as: D. A. Shah, “Scoring conventions reorder adaptation policies in streaming anomaly detection,” Zenodo, 2026, doi:10.5281/zenodo.22333125.

Abstract

A streaming anomaly detector has to decide when to rebuild itself once its input starts to drift. We compare four ways of handling that, keeping everything else the same: never rebuild, keep learning all the time, rebuild on a schedule, or rebuild when a drift detector goes off. We scored the same runs under four published conventions and got 4 different winners. Same predictions, too. HST, drift comes 8th of 10 under point-wise F1 and 2nd under the composite F-score. The comparison covers 10 seeds and the 15 source recordings that have a fault in them, with paired tests and Holm correction. We also pull apart two things that usually get lumped together: the anomaly model and the adaptation policy. On this data, the best policy is whichever one your scoring happens to favour. Every one of the 10 strategies changes rank between point-wise and composite scoring, and the biggest jump is 6 places. Then there's a third dataset, the UCR Anomaly Archive, which was built to replace benchmarks its authors thought were flawed. There, none of this matters much. No policy stands out from the rest, and by the archive's own threshold-free test the best of the ten puts its peak score inside the labelled window on 0.12 of series. Code, logs and every table here come back from a single command.

Introduction

A detector trained once on a sensor stream goes wrong in one of two directions as the process it watches changes. If it never updates, ordinary operation drifts away from what it learned and it flags almost everything. If it updates continuously, it absorbs the change into its own idea of normal and goes quiet, so a fault that arrives slowly is learned rather than reported. Both failures are easy to build by accident and neither is visible in a single accuracy number.

The question this raises is not whether anomalies can be detected but when the detector should update itself. That question has an established shape: monitor the input, and when a change-detection test fires, rebuild. What it does not have is an established answer, because the evidence for one policy over another is usually a single number from a single run, scored under whichever convention the authors preferred.

We built the comparison carefully enough to find out, and the result was not the one we set out to report. Our own earlier version of this work, run once at one seed and scored point-wise, concluded that a periodic rebuild schedule was best and that the continuously-learning control was broken. Both conclusions turned out to be properties of the scoring convention, not of the detectors. Under event-level scoring the control catches every fault in the stream, and the ranking of the policies rearranges.

This paper reports that finding properly. Our contributions:

  1. A convention-crossed comparison. The same runs are scored under point-wise F1, the composite F-score of Garg et al. (2021), range-based precision and recall (Tatbul et al., 2018), and point-adjust (Xu et al., 2018) with its PA%K repair (Kim et al., 2022). The conventions disagree about which adaptation policy is best.
  2. A factorial design. Adaptation policy and anomaly model are crossed, so a difference can be attributed to one or the other. The usual presentation compares a static Isolation Forest against an adaptive Half-Space Trees model and calls the difference adaptation.
  3. Replication and paired tests. Every result is repeated over 10 seeds and over the 15 source recordings that carry a fault. Comparisons are paired within a seed and within a recording, with Holm correction over the family of comparisons we report.
  4. Negative results stated as such. Whether a strategy beats the F1 obtained by flagging every single row is itself convention-dependent: 7 of 10 clear it point-wise, 10 under the composite score, and 3 under range-based scoring (only 2 with the whole interval above the baseline). We report the baseline beside every result, and did not go looking for the convention that flatters ours.

Related work

Adapting to concept drift.

Gama and Žliobaitė (2014) organise the field into detectors that signal a change and learners that respond to one. ADWIN (Bifet and Gavaldà, 2007) keeps a window it cuts whenever two sub-windows differ enough in mean, which gives it a change point without a fixed window size. KSWIN (Raab et al., 2020) runs a Kolmogorov-Smirnov test between a reference sample and a sliding one. The Page-Hinkley test (Page, 1954) integrates a one-sided deviation and fires when the running sum exceeds a threshold. Larger comparisons of detectors exist (Barros and Santos, 2018), though they are usually framed around supervised classification error, not the unlabelled input statistic this project watches. The section “Drift monitoring” gives the reason for watching the input at all.

Streaming anomaly detection.

Half-Space Trees (Tan et al., 2011) score a point by the mass of the region it falls into, over an ensemble of random trees with fixed feature ranges, and update in constant time per observation. Isolation Forest (Liu et al., 2008) isolates points by random splits and is the usual static baseline. Local Outlier Factor (Breunig et al., 2000), the one-class SVM (Schölkopf et al., 2001) and the minimum covariance determinant estimator (Rousseeuw and van Driessen, 1999) are the classical alternatives; none supports an incremental update, so for them adaptation can only mean a refit. More recent systems adapt by pooling models without resetting one (Yoon et al., 2022). We use the simpler reset because the object of study here is the policy, not the model.

How these systems are scored.

This is where the field is least settled, and it is the part our results turn on. Point-wise F1 treats every row independently and rewards a detector for flagging every row of a long fault, which is not what an operator wants. Xu et al. (2018) introduced point-adjust, under which one flagged row inside a true segment credits the detector with the whole segment; Kim et al. (2022) showed that this inflates scores so far that random predictions beat published models, and proposed PA%K, which only credits a segment when at least K of it was flagged. Tatbul et al. (2018) give a range-based precision and recall that scores existence, overlap and fragmentation separately. Garg et al. (2021) define a composite F-score that pairs point-wise precision with event-level recall. Paparrizos et al. (2022) and Huet et al. (2022) propose further alternatives. Wu and Keogh (2023) argue that several widely-used benchmarks, including the one we use as a second dataset, are flawed enough to create an illusion of progress.

Our position is narrower than a survey of these proposals. We take four of them as given, apply them to one set of runs, and report that they do not agree about which adaptation policy to use. The disagreement is the result; we are not arguing that any one of the four is correct.

Setup

Adaptation policies

Every policy sees the same stream, the same warm-up length and the same alarm threshold. The only thing that differs is when, or whether, the model is rebuilt.

never
The model is fitted once on the warm-up window and left alone.
online
The model keeps learning from every row and is never explicitly rebuilt. It is a control and not a policy, and it matters: without it, never and periodic would differ in the model as well as the schedule.
periodic
The model is rebuilt every 1,000 rows, whether or not anything has changed.
drift
The model is rebuilt when a drift monitor fires on the input.

Rebuilding always means the same operation: re-run warm-up on the most recent 1,000 rows, which regenerates the model, its feature ranges and its threshold together. Between rebuilds every policy except online holds the model fixed. A retraining policy that also learns continuously is not really a retraining policy, and in an earlier version of this work it collapsed into the control.

Models

Half-Space Trees is the online model. Isolation Forest, LOF, the one-class SVM and the MCD estimator are the static ones. Crossing the models with the policies gives the grid in Table 1; the three classical baselines appear only under never, since they cannot be updated incrementally.

Two implementation choices are worth stating because they are what makes the comparison mean anything. Feature ranges are fixed at warm-up and never rolled forward. The usual choice is a min-max scaler, but it adapts continuously and would absorb the drift before the model ever saw it, hiding the effect being measured. The alarm threshold is likewise a quantile of the warm-up scores, held until the next rebuild. Half-Space Trees normalises its raw score against a maximum that is essentially never reached, so scores sit in a narrow offset band and an absolute threshold is meaningless.

Drift monitoring

The drift monitor watches the input, not the model's anomaly score. Watching the score is self-defeating for a learning model: it accommodates the shift, its score distribution does not move, and the detector never fires. In an earlier run that produced zero detections on the labelled stream. The monitored signal is the mean absolute z-score of the sensors, standardised against the window the model was last built on, so it answers “has the world moved since this model was built”. The reference is refit on every rebuild.

Because the schedule depends only on this input statistic, it is computed in one cheap pass and the scoring is done afterwards in blocks; a test asserts that this gives the same flags, scores and adaptation points as the plain loop.

Thresholds

The alarm threshold is a quantile of the warm-up score distribution. It encodes how often anomalies are expected, and the dataset families here differ by more than an order of magnitude in base rate, so a single value across all of them would not be a fair comparison but a badly calibrated detector on most. We use q=0.50 on the labelled SKAB stream, which is 34.4% anomalous, and q=0.98 on the injected, NAB and UCR streams. The section “Transferring the calibration” measures what carrying one setting to a new dataset costs.

Evaluation conventions

We score every run four ways. Let the ground truth be a set of contiguous events and the prediction a set of flagged rows.

Point-wise.

Precision, recall and F1 over rows, each scored independently.

Composite.

Point-wise precision with event-level recall: an event counts as recalled if any row inside it was flagged, while precision still pays for every false row. This is the composite F-score of Garg et al. (2021). We arrived at it independently before finding it in the literature, and our test suite asserts that the two definitions agree.

Range-based.

The precision and recall of Tatbul et al. (2018), with a flat positional bias and the reciprocal cardinality factor, so a true range detected in many fragments scores below the same coverage detected in one. We report α = 0, pure overlap, and give α = 1, pure existence, as a sensitivity.

Point-adjust.

The convention of Xu et al. (2018), and PA%K at K=0.2 (Kim et al., 2022). We report point-adjust to show what it does to our ranking, and we do not rely on it. On SKAB's fault blocks, which average about 390 rows, crediting a whole block for one flagged row is a very large gift.

Every result is quoted against the F1 obtained by flagging every single row, which at a base rate b is 2b/(1+b). On the labelled stream that is 0.512. An F1 in the low 0.5s means nothing next to it, and reporting one without it would be misleading.

Experimental design

Data

SKAB (Katser and Kozitsin, 2020) is a labelled industrial testbed with eight sensors. Our labelled stream concatenates 16 valve1 recordings, giving 17,160 scored rows at a 34.4% anomaly rate; the individual recordings are too short to warm up on and still leave stream to measure. 15 of the 16 contain a labelled fault and are scored separately in the section “Does the ranking survive the data?”; the remaining one has none, and an F1 on it would be zero for every strategy alike. The joins between recordings are real regime changes of unknown size, so this stream is used for anomaly quality only and never for drift timing.

Injected streams are built by applying a known shift to SKAB's anomaly-free recording in four shapes: sudden, incremental, gradual and recurring. They contain no true anomalies by construction, which is what makes them useful: change points are known to the row, so timing is exact, and every flag raised is by definition a false alarm.

NAB (Lavin and Ahmad, 2015) is the second dataset, used to test whether a calibration transfers. It differs from SKAB in the ways that would break one: it is univariate where SKAB has eight sensors, and roughly 10% anomalous where SKAB is 34.4%. We use 6 series long enough to warm up on.

The UCR Anomaly Archive (Wu and Keogh, 2023) is the third. Its authors argued that NAB and benchmarks like it are flawed enough to create an illusion of progress, and built the archive as a replacement: 250 univariate series, each with exactly one anomaly and a clean training prefix. That is what SKAB lacks. On SKAB every strategy catches every labelled event, so event-level recall is 1.0 for all of them; with one short anomaly per series, the proportion found becomes a measurement and not a constant.

The full archive at 10 seeds is too much for one core, so we take 8 series under a rule fixed in advance (data_loader.select_ucr_series): at most 12,000 rows, a clean prefix longer than the warm-up window, an anomaly under a tenth of the series, and at most one series per source signal, in archive-index order. The last condition matters because the archive's 251 files cover only 42 source signals under varied names; without it, our first subset was mostly two signals. 8 is also where the archive divides: the next-shortest distinct signal is 24,667 rows long. The selected series average 8,392 rows at a 1.05% anomaly rate, which puts the trivial baseline at 0.020 against 0.512 on SKAB.

Replication and pairing

Each run is repeated at 10 seeds. A seed drives the model, the drift detector where it samples, and the gradual injection, the only stream that draws randomly. Runs are paired: at a given seed every strategy sees the same stream and the same warm-up, which matters because the between-seed spread is larger than the gap between policies.

The second unit of replication is the more informative one. Every strategy is also scored on each of the 15 source recordings that contain a fault. Seeds ask whether a gap survives the randomness; recordings ask whether it survives the data. A policy that is stable across seeds and unstable across recordings has not been shown to work.

Statistics

Intervals are percentile bootstrap intervals over 10,000 resamples (Efron, 1979). Comparisons use the Wilcoxon signed-rank test (Wilcoxon, 1945) on the paired differences, in place of a t-test, because the metrics are bounded, skewed and occasionally pinned at 0 or 1. We apply Holm-Bonferroni correction (Holm, 1979) within each stream, over the family of comparisons the paper actually makes.

One caveat is built into the reporting. With n paired samples the smallest attainable two-sided p from the exact signed-rank test is 2/2^n, so below six pairs no effect of any size can reach p<0.05. Comparisons below that threshold are flagged as underpowered and never counted as significant, because a non-significant verdict there is a property of n and not of the data (Demšar, 2006).

The models come from river (Montiel et al., 2021) and scikit-learn (Pedregosa et al., 2011), and the full grid runs on one laptop core in under an hour.

Results

The convention decides the ranking

Table 1 scores one set of runs four ways. The predictions are identical down the row; only the function applied to them changes.

The four conventions produce 4 different winners. Point-wise F1 puts iForest, drift first at 0.539; the composite F-score puts HST, periodic first at 0.606; range-based scoring puts iForest, periodic first at 0.198. 10 of 10 strategies change rank between point-wise and composite scoring, and the largest single move is 6 places. HST, drift is the clearest case: it places 8th under point-wise F1 and 2nd under the composite score, on the same flags.

Figure 1 shows why, and Figure 2 draws the same reordering as a bump chart. Point-wise recall rewards a detector for flagging every row of a long fault, and SKAB's faults average about 390 rows, so a detector that flags each fault sparsely is punished for exactly the behaviour an operator wants. Event-level recall asks instead whether each fault was noticed at all. Neither is wrong. They are answers to different questions, and which one is asked decides the ranking.

Point-adjust is shown but not relied on: it credits an entire 390-row fault block for one flagged row, which inflates every strategy at once, as Kim et al. (2022) warned.

The last column of Table 1 is the one to read first. 7 of 10 strategies clear the flag-everything baseline under point-wise scoring and 10 clear it under the composite score. A detector that flags 99% of rows scores near the baseline by construction, and several of the static baselines do exactly that.

Range-based scoring moves the baseline as well as the detectors, and it is worth saying where it lands. Flagging every row produces one predicted range spanning the stream, so its precision is divided by the number of true events that range swallows, and the trivial baseline drops to 0.045. Against that, 3 of 10 strategies clear it on the mean, but only 2 do so with their whole interval above the baseline; the other, HST, periodic, scores 0.0454 against 0.0449, a margin well inside its own interval. The detectors are charged in the opposite direction: a permissive policy emits thousands of short predicted ranges across each fault, and the cardinality factor bills it for every fragment. Fragmentation is invisible to the other three conventions and decisive under this one.

Model against policy

The usual presentation of this comparison contrasts a static Isolation Forest against an adaptive Half-Space Trees model, which confounds the two factors. Figure 3 crosses them.

Reading down a column separates the model from the policy, and reading across a row separates the policy from the model. Both factors move the score, and the policy moves it further: under the composite view the spread across policies within Half-Space Trees is wider than the spread across models within the never column. The three classical baselines sit at the bottom of that column together, all of them flagging over 99% of rows, which is the same failure the static Isolation Forest shows and not a quirk of one model.

One baseline needed help. The MCD estimator assumes one elliptical cloud of normal data, and on one NAB series 859 of the 1,000 warm-up rows are exactly 0.0, which makes its covariance singular; we widen its support fraction until it fits.

Does the ranking survive the data?

Seeds test whether a gap survives the randomness. They do not test whether it survives a different recording, and on this data that is the harder question. Figure 4 scores every strategy separately on each of the 15 source recordings that contain a fault.

Table 2 reports the paired comparisons under the composite score, over both units. Of 48 comparisons on the labelled stream across all conventions, 36 survive Holm correction; most of the ones that do not are comparisons over recordings.

The between-recording spread is wide enough that a gap of a few hundredths, reported from one run, says nothing about which policy to deploy. It also complicates the aggregate ranking. HST, periodic, which wins Table 1 on the mean, fails to beat the trivial baseline on 4 of the 15 recordings, and its interquartile range in Figure 4 straddles zero. iForest, periodic scores lower on average but fails on 0 of them, with an interquartile range entirely above zero. Which one to prefer depends on whether the operator is averaging over many streams or deploying on one.

Drift detectors and detection timing

The injected streams are where timing can be measured, because the change point is known to the row and nothing in the stream is genuinely anomalous. Table 3 reports the delay at a 3 sd shift.

Figure 5 plots the same measurement against magnitude. Two shapes separate the detectors. A sudden step is caught quickly by anything that watches the mean. Gradual drift, where the two regimes interleave before the mean has moved, is the case a location detector cannot see: early in the transition individual rows flip between the old and new regime, so the signal grows spiky before its level changes. Feeding ADWIN the trailing variance of the monitored statistic, in place of its level, reacts to that. It cuts the gradual delay by more than half, and it pays for that by going blind to a smooth ramp, which shifts the mean without changing the spread: on the incremental shape it never fires at all, at any magnitude. Running a mean ADWIN and a variance ADWIN together and firing when either does recovers every shape and keeps the better gradual delay.

Page-Hinkley is the quickest of the five on the sudden and recurring shapes and raises fewer false alarms than ADWIN, but it is the slowest detector that fires at all on the incremental ramp: a cumulative sum needs the deviation to accumulate, and a slow ramp supplies it slowly. KSWIN is slower than ADWIN on every shape and raises the most false alarms. The false-alarm column is an upper bound, for the reason given in the section “Limitations”.

Transferring the calibration

Everything above is tuned on one industrial rig, which invites the objection that the settings are fitted to it. Table 4 applies the SKAB threshold to 6 NAB series unchanged. NAB is univariate where SKAB has eight sensors, and roughly 10% anomalous where SKAB is 34.4%, so it breaks a transferred calibration in the ways that matter.

The metric effect reappears here and is larger than on SKAB. Under point-wise scoring the transferred setting beats the trivial baseline on 3 of 6 series; under composite scoring it beats it on 6. NAB's anomalies are short and sparse, so point-wise recall penalises a detector that flags a window without also flagging its neighbourhood, which is the behaviour the composite score is built to credit. What does not carry is any particular strategy. 5 different strategies take the top place across the 6 series, and one of them is a classical static baseline, so the threshold has to be set per deployment.

Where event recall discriminates

On SKAB every strategy catches every labelled event, so composite F1 is a ranking on precision alone. The UCR subset supplies the missing axis: one anomaly per series, so a strategy either finds each one or it does not.

The proportion of anomalies found (Table 5) runs from 0.25 for OC-SVM, never to 0.50 for LOF, never, a real spread that SKAB cannot show at all. The level matters more: not one of the ten finds most of the anomalies, on a subset chosen for being short and tractable. Against a trivial baseline of 0.020, 8 of 10 strategies clear it under the composite score and 1 point-wise, by margins too small to mean much.

The archive's own criterion.

The archive's authors score a series as solved when the single highest anomaly score falls inside the labelled window, which needs no threshold. Substituting our convention for theirs would be the move this paper criticises, so Table 5 reports both. Under the archive's criterion the best strategies, tied, are MCD, never; OC-SVM, never; and LOF, never, each at 0.12; the worst manages 0.00, and the average across all ten is 0.06. None of the strategies at the top of that list is the one with the best composite score, so the two protocols do not agree on a winner either.

Adaptation does not help here.

The best composite score on this data belongs to iForest, never, and the most anomalies are found by LOF, never. Both are configured to never rebuild, and neither is one of the 4 adaptive configurations. On the benchmark built to be hard, the question this paper is about stops mattering: the policies are separated by less than the noise, and the classical static detectors are as good as anything with a rebuild schedule.

Sensitivity to the constants we chose

Three values in this design were picked by judgement: the warm-up length of 1,000 rows, the 750-step horizon within which a detection is credited to a change point, and the 250-step cooldown after a detector fires. Figure 6 varies the first two.

The matching horizon is not load-bearing: past 500 steps the mean delay is identical for every drift shape. Warm-up length does matter, and unevenly: the periodic schedule improves steadily as the warm-up lengthens, the drift-triggered one is flat, and the static baseline moves erratically. We treat this as a sensitivity, not a tuning result, because changing the warm-up also changes which rows are scored and so moves the base rate. The cooldown changes the number of rebuilds only at its longest setting, and none of the conclusions above depends on it.

Cost

On one laptop core the slowest strategy, iForest, drift, processes 844 rows per second and the fastest, OC-SVM, never, 129,212, a factor of about 153. Most of that gap is implementation: Half-Space Trees is scored one observation at a time in river, the scikit-learn baselines in vectorised blocks. Every strategy keeps up with a single sensor rig; per-strategy figures are in results/throughput.csv.

Discussion

What a practitioner should take from this

First, on this data the choice of scoring convention moves the answer more than the choice of adaptation policy, so it should be made deliberately and stated. It follows from what an alarm costs. If an operator investigates each alarm, every false row is paid for and point-wise precision is what matters; if they investigate each episode, a detector that flags one row of a fault has done its job and the composite or range-based view fits better.

Second, quote a trivial baseline next to every score. At a base rate of 34.4%, flagging every row scores 0.512 under point-wise F1, so a detector can clear 0.5 F1 while doing nothing at all.

Third, a mean over streams answers a question about a benchmark, while an operator with one stream is asking about that stream. The strategy that wins our headline table on the mean is not the one we would deploy, for the per-recording reason given in the section “Does the ranking survive the data?”.

On the adaptation question itself

Stripped of the metric problem, the practical picture is narrower than “adaptive detection works better”. Rebuilding on a schedule and rebuilding on detected change both beat leaving the model alone, and the margin between the two is small next to the margin between either of them and the trivial baseline. The case for drift-triggered rebuilding is not that it scores higher. It is that it reacts to evidence and not to a clock, which lets it notice a sudden shift within a few rows instead of waiting for the next scheduled rebuild, and keeps it from rebuilding on a stream that has not moved.

That is a claim about the shape of the response, measured in the section “Drift detectors and detection timing”, and a smaller one than we expected to make.

Limitations

The base recording is not stationary.

SKAB's anomaly-free recording has no annotated faults but the process drifts on its own. Running with no injected drift still produces adaptations, at nearly the same positions as with a 3 sd step injected. False-alarm counts on the injected streams are therefore an upper bound and not a measurement: some of those firings are the detector correctly noticing real process change for which we have no ground truth. For the same reason we do not report detection rate, which comes out at 1.0 for every magnitude including the zero control, because a firing always lands within the matching horizon of an arbitrary point.

The labelled stream is concatenated.

The individual valve1 recordings are too short to warm up on, so we join 16 of them, and the joins are regime changes of unknown size. The stream is therefore never used for drift timing, and the per-recording results avoid the joins.

Event recall saturates on SKAB.

On SKAB every strategy catches every event, so the recall axis carries no information there. The UCR subset (the section “Where event recall discriminates”) is what bounds this limitation: it applies to SKAB, partly to NAB, and not to UCR.

Three datasets, one of them contested.

Wu and Keogh (2023) argue that NAB and benchmarks like it are flawed enough to mislead. We use NAB only to ask whether a calibration transfers, which is a weaker use than ranking detectors on it, but the criticism still applies to the section “Transferring the calibration”. The UCR subset is only 8 of 250 series, chosen by a stated rule and bounded by what one core can run; all 250 would be a stronger test.

No deep or model-pooling baselines.

The autoencoder and model-pooling systems that lead recent leaderboards (Yoon et al., 2022) are not included. Our claim is about how adaptation policies compare under different conventions, not about raw detection quality, and the metric result matters more for those systems, which are usually reported under point-adjust.

Threshold and hardware.

The threshold has to be set from the expected anomaly rate of each stream; we measured what carrying one setting across datasets costs, but no rule here removes that choice. Throughput comes from one laptop core and two libraries, so it supports statements about relative cost only.

Reproducing this

Every number in this paper, including those in the prose, is generated from the committed CSV files by scripts/make_paper_tables.py; the manuscript contains no hand-typed values. The repository README lists the commands that regenerate the experiments, figures and tables, and the test suite checks the metric implementations against hand-computed values.

Conclusion

We compared four adaptation policies for a streaming anomaly detector, crossed with the model they run on, repeated over 10 seeds and 15 recordings, and scored the same runs under four published conventions. The four conventions produce 4 different winners.

The narrow finding is about one benchmark and one family of detectors. The general one is that a paper reporting a single scoring convention has not established which policy is better, only which policy that convention prefers. On the stream studied here, HST, drift moves from 8th to 2nd of 10 on identical predictions.

The third dataset put a limit on all of it. On the UCR subset no policy separates from the others, the classical static detectors match anything with a rebuild schedule, and under the archive's own criterion the field as a whole puts its peak score inside the labelled window on 0.06 of series. The comparison this paper is built around is worth making on SKAB and is close to meaningless on the benchmark built to be hard. We would rather finish on that than on the part that worked.
